text: Customers who open our emails spend more. Weeks with higher ad spend have higher sales. Users who use feature X churn less. Each is a statement about correlation, and each tempts us to act as if one thing causes the other. Sometimes it does. Often it doesn't. This lesson gives you the vocabulary and the Python tools to tell the difference.

The Pearson correlation coefficient, r, summarizes how closely two numeric variables follow a straight-line pattern — ranging from negative 1, a perfect downward line, through 0, no linear pattern, to positive 1, a perfect upward line. Its size describes strength, its sign describes direction, and it says absolutely nothing about which variable drives the other, or whether either does.

A correlation from a small sample can look strong by pure luck, and with huge samples, even a trivially small r can be statistically significant. Spearman correlation works on ranks instead, and is better when a relationship is consistently increasing or decreasing but curved, or when outliers are a concern.

Imagine a year of daily data where holiday season pushes up both advertising spend and sales, but in this simulation ads have no effect at all on sales — only season matters. The correlation between ads and sales comes out to 0.819 with a vanishingly small p-value. A dashboard would proudly report ad spend strongly predicts sales, and a manager might double the budget.

But the strong relationship arises because season is a confounder — a variable that influences both. If you've measured the confounder, you can remove its influence from both variables and correlate what's left: regress each variable on season, then correlate the residuals, the parts season doesn't explain.

Once season is accounted for, the correlation collapses to essentially zero, 0.009 — matching exactly how we built the data. The catch: this only works for confounders you thought of and actually measured. Unmeasured ones stay hidden, which is why adjustment alone rarely proves causation.

Suppose instead that ad spend is set by lottery, completely independent of the season. The correlation between random spend and sales vanishes to 0.026, because randomly assigned spend can't be tied to the season, or to anything else. This is the logic of the randomized controlled experiment, and why A/B tests are the gold standard — random assignment cancels out every confounder, measured or not.

Correlation can also miss real relationships entirely — r only captures straight-line association. A perfect U-shaped relationship, where y is almost entirely determined by x, can still give r near zero — here just negative 0.165, even though x fully determines y. Always plot the data before trusting a correlation number.

When two variables move together, consider four explanations: X causes Y; Y causes X, reverse causation; a third variable causes both, confounding; or plain coincidence, especially if you searched many pairs. Often more than one applies at once.

Randomized experiments are the strongest path to causation. When you can't randomize, rely on careful design — measuring and adjusting for likely confounders, comparing before and after a change, exploiting natural experiments, building a plausible mechanism. Even then, hedge your claims — associated with is honest, causes needs evidence beyond correlation. To recap: correlation measures linear association, confounders create misleading correlations, adjustment only helps for what you measured, and randomization handles the rest.
